title: A betting board with a bankroll
objectives: Track P&L and size bets across a board of bets under a bankroll limit.

screens.title: A board of bets
screens.prose: An interviewer lays out four bets on separate coins and dice. You have £100. You may stake any amount on any bet, or none.

state.caption: Odds of b to 1 pay £b for each £1 staked

screens.question: Which bet should you not take at all?

options.why: You skipped a real edge. At evens, 0.55 wins 10p per £1 on average.
You judged by the win chance. At 2 to 1, 0.4 wins 20p per £1 on average.
You took c for its payout. At 3 to 1 a chance of 0.2 loses 20p per £1.

hints.text: Work out each bet's average gain per £1: $p \times b - (1 - p)$.
c loses 20p per £1 on average: skip it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the bet whose average gain per £1 is negative.

byKey.none: You took c for its payout. At 3 to 1 a chance of 0.2 loses 20p per £1.
byKey.b: You judged by the win chance. At 2 to 1, 0.4 wins 20p per £1 on average.

explain.text: A big payout is not an edge. c pays 3 to 1 but wins only one time in five: −£0.20 per £1. The other three bets each gain on average.

screens.title: Edge per pound
screens.prose: The edge of a bet is its average gain per £1 staked: $p\,b - (1 - p)$.
screens.question: Fill the edge of each bet.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Edge is $p\,b - (1 - p)$.

explain.text: b and d have the same edge, 0.2, though b pays more. Edge measures the bet; odds measure how lumpy it is. Kelly needs both.

screens.title: Kelly on each bet
screens.prose: Stake each bet at its Kelly fraction of the bankroll, $f^* = p - (1 - p)/b$, and stake nothing when $f^*$ is negative.
screens.question: Fill each stake on £100, in pounds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $f^* = p - (1 - p)/b$, times £100.

explain.text: a and b each get 0.1 of the bankroll, d gets 0.2, and c nothing. b's edge is twice a's, but its odds are twice too, so Kelly stakes them equally. Edge over odds sets the size.

screens.title: What the board earns
screens.prose: With stakes of £10, £10, £0 and £20, each bet earns its stake times its edge on average.
screens.question: What is the board's expected profit this round, in pounds?

hints.text: Multiply each stake by its edge.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add stake times edge for each bet.

byKey.stakes: That is the total staked, not the expected profit.
byKey.withc: You staked £10 on c. Its edge is negative.

explain.text: a earns £1, b £2 and d £4 on average: £7 on £40 staked. c would only subtract. The round's result will swing around that £7.

screens.title: A limit on the round
screens.prose: The interviewer adds a rule: at most £30 at risk in a round. Your Kelly stakes total £40. Scale every stake down by the same factor.

derive.caption: Total at risk: £{{fixed(values.a + values.b + values.c + values.d, 2)}}

screens.question: Set the stakes on a, b and d so that £30 is at risk.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply every stake by $30/40 = 0.75$.

byKey.cutd: You cut only the largest stake. Scale them all by 0.75, so the mix stays the same.

explain.text: Scaling by 0.75 keeps each bet's share of the risk. The stakes become £7.50, £7.50 and £15. Cutting one bet alone would change the mix Kelly chose.

screens.title: The capped board
screens.prose: With the cap, the stakes are £7.50, £7.50, £0 and £15.
screens.question: What is the expected profit now, in pounds?

hints.text: Every stake fell by a quarter.

byKey.sub: You subtracted the £10 cut. Scale the profit instead.

explain.text: $0.75 \times 7 = 5.25$, or $0.75 + 1.50 + 3.00$ bet by bet. The cap costs £1.75 of expected profit a round. It buys smaller swings.

screens.title: Round one
screens.prose: Back to full Kelly, no cap: £10 on a, £10 on b, £20 on d. The results: a wins, b loses, d wins.
screens.question: What is your bankroll after the round, in pounds?

hints.text: At evens a win pays the stake; a loss loses it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add each bet's result to £100.

byKey.pnl: That is the round's profit. Add it to £100.
byKey.bwin: You counted b as a win at 2 to 1. It lost.

explain.text: a and d win £10 and £20; b loses £10. The round makes £20 and the bankroll is £120. Every stake next round is a fraction of £120.

screens.title: Same stakes again?
screens.prose: Your bankroll is now £{{carry.bank|120}}. A friend says: "Keep the stakes you had: £10, £10 and £20. They worked."
screens.question: What do you stake on d this round, in pounds, using a bankroll of £120?

hints.text: Kelly is a fraction of the current bankroll.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Stake 0.2 of the bankroll you have now.

byKey.kept: You kept the old stake. Kelly rescales with the bankroll after every round.
byKey.all: You staked the bankroll. One loss would end the game.
byKey.profit: You staked 0.2 of the profit only.

explain.text: Kelly stakes a fraction of what you have now: £24 on d, £12 each on a and b. After a loss the stakes shrink just as they grew. Keeping old stakes drifts away from the fraction.

screens.title: Round two
screens.prose: From £120 the stakes are £12, £12, £0 and £24. This time a loses, b wins at 2 to 1, and d loses.
screens.question: What is the bankroll after round two, in pounds?

hints.text: b at 2 to 1 wins twice its stake.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. a loses 12, b wins 24, d loses 24.

byKey.evens: You paid b at evens. At 2 to 1 it wins £24.
byKey.fixed: You used the old stakes, £10, £10 and £20.

explain.text: The round loses £12, and the bankroll falls from £120 to £108. Next round the stakes shrink to £10.80, £10.80 and £21.60. Sizing to the bankroll makes ruin impossible, though the swings are real.

screens.title: Sizing a board
screens.prose:
For each bet, $f^* = p - (1 - p)/b$; skip it when $f^* \le 0$. If the stakes total more than the cap $C$, scale every one by $C / \sum f^* W$:
$$\text{stake}_i = f_i^* \, W \times \min\!\left(1, \frac{C}{\sum_j f_j^* W}\right).$$
screens.question: A bet at 3 to 1 with chance 0.3, on a bankroll of £120. What is its Kelly stake, in pounds?

byKey.edge: You staked the edge, 0.2, times 120. Divide the edge by the odds.

explain.text: $f^* = 1/15$, so £8 of £120. The edge is $0.3 \times 3 - 0.7 = 0.2$, and dividing by the odds 3 gives the fraction. Here bets are sized one at a time; joint Kelly for bets settled together is a little lower.

screens.title: The board in code
screens.prose: Code the stakes and the ledger. `run_board` restakes from the current bankroll each round, as you did by hand.
screens.question: Complete `board_stakes` and `run_board`.

widget.solution:
def board_stakes(bets, bankroll, cap):
    """bets: list of (b, p) for b-to-1 odds and win chance p.
    Kelly stake on each, 0 without an edge, all scaled down
    together if they total more than cap."""
    stakes = [max(0.0, p - (1 - p) / b) * bankroll for b, p in bets]
    total = sum(stakes)
    if total > cap:
        stakes = [s * cap / total for s in stakes]
    return stakes


def run_board(bets, outcomes, bankroll, cap):
    """outcomes: one list of True/False per round, one per bet.
    Restake from the current bankroll each round.
    Return [(start, profit, end), ...], one row a round."""
    rows = []
    for won in outcomes:
        stakes = board_stakes(bets, bankroll, cap)
        profit = sum(s * b if w else -s
                     for s, (b, p), w in zip(stakes, bets, won))
        rows.append((bankroll, profit, bankroll + profit))
        bankroll += profit
    return rows

tests.call: run_board([(1, 0.55), (2, 0.4), (3, 0.2), (1, 0.6)], [[True, False, False, True], [False, True, False, False]], 100, 1000)

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. Stakes and ledger rows are compared within 1e-9.

hints.text: Clamp each Kelly fraction at 0 before multiplying by the bankroll.
Scale only when the total is above the cap.
In `run_board`, a win pays `stake * b`; a loss costs the stake.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the clamp, the cap and the payout at odds.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: The two rounds give £120 then £108, as on the screens. With the cap and every bet winning, the board makes £37.50 on £30 at risk. A zero-edge bet, evens at 0.5, gets a stake of 0.

screens.title: A book under a limit
screens.prose: A trader runs positions sized at 10% of the desk's capital for each idea. After a bad month the capital falls from £1,000,000 to £800,000.
screens.question: What is the new size for one idea, in pounds?

hints.text: Size is a fraction of current capital.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 10% of the capital you have now.

byKey.old: You kept the old size. The capital fell, so the size falls with it.
byKey.cut: You cut by the whole £200,000 loss twice over. Take 10% of £800,000.

explain.text: Each idea shrinks from £100,000 to £80,000, as Kelly stakes shrink after a loss. Resizing keeps risk in line with what can be lost. Desks do this by rule, not by feel.

ideas: Stake each bet at $f^* = p - (1 - p)/b$ of the current bankroll, and skip bets with no edge.
When the stakes break the limit, scale them all alike: £40 capped at £30 means 0.75 of each.
Restake every round from the bankroll you have: £100, then £120, then £108.

formula.name: Kelly on a board
formula.note: $W$ the bankroll, $C$ the cap on money at risk.

summary.trap: Backing a bet for its big payout, or keeping last round's stakes after the bankroll has moved.

quiz.prose: A bet at evens wins with chance 0.5. Your bankroll is £200.
quiz.question: What is the Kelly stake, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no edge, Kelly stakes nothing.

byKey.half: You staked the win chance. With no edge there is nothing to grow.
byKey.some: You staked a little for fun. Any stake adds risk with no gain.

explain.text: $f^* = 0.5 - 0.5/1 = 0$. A fair bet adds risk and no growth. Kelly skips it.

quiz.prose: The board of four bets on £100, at half Kelly.
quiz.question: What do you stake on d, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve the full Kelly stake of £20.

byKey.full: That is full Kelly. Half Kelly halves it.

explain.text: Half Kelly stakes £5, £5, £0 and £10. It gives up a little growth for much smaller swings. Many traders prefer it because their $p$ is only an estimate.

quiz.prose: A board on £200: evens with chance 0.6, and 4 to 1 with chance 0.25. No cap.
quiz.question: What is the board's expected profit, in pounds?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each Kelly stake, then stake times edge.

byKey.one: You counted only the evens bet.
